module: Mark synthetic outputs and verify detection

lesson.title: Use the Code and build proportionate evidence
lesson.summary: Understand Code adequacy and maintain evidence of implemented marking and disclosure measures.

prerequisites.reason: The learner must distinguish operative law from interpretation and voluntary methods.
The learner must preserve other applicable duties when applying this transparency rule.
The learner must evaluate the four legal qualities before judging a method or supplier.
The learner must retain the product provider’s responsibility through upstream handoffs.

blocks: Article 50(7) says the **Commission** encourages and facilitates Union-level Codes for detection, marking and labelling. Under the amended provision it assesses adequacy taking utmost account of the Board's opinion, through Article 56(6)'s procedure.

If a Code is inadequate, the Commission may adopt an implementing act specifying common implementation rules through Article 98(2). Older documents describe the previous assessment procedure; do not replace amended law with that earlier account.

sources.title: AI Act, 27 July 2026 baseline: Article 50(7), Article 56(6); Guidelines paragraphs 146-150
Commission Article 50 Guidelines C(2026) 5054 final; non-binding interpretation
Final Transparency Code, 10 June 2026; voluntary implementation framework
Commission Opinion C(2026) 4839 final, conclusion 52: adequacy assessment

blocks: The final Transparency Code has a provider section for marking/detection and a deployer section for deepfakes and specified published text. It is not a complete implementation manual for every Article 50 activity.

The Commission's July adequacy assessment concludes it supports effective implementation of paragraphs 2, 4 and 5. Adherence is not conclusive evidence of compliance. Authorities can still examine whether the measures were actually implemented.

blocks: Signing is voluntary. Within the Code, **will** identifies mandatory commitments for the route a signatory relies on; **encouraged** identifies optional recommended measures; **may** permits optional measures or implementation flexibility.

For example, richer provenance information and additional forensic detection are encouraged or optional in the provider section. Do not convert those recommendations into standalone statutory requirements for everyone.

blocks: **Compliance evidence** shows how the implementation meets the duty: a high-level process description, tests, limitations, preservation and detection arrangements, responsible people and maintenance.

The Code's provider section requires ongoing testing and verification proportionate to circumstances. Its deployer section addresses internal processes, awareness, feedback, correction of substantiated mislabelling and cooperation with authorities.

blocks: Harbour's supplier has signed, but its detector is unavailable and no export test exists. A signature cannot fill those evidential gaps. Keep a documented correction process and retest when the implementation changes.

Non-signatories can demonstrate compliance by adequate alternative means. Commission guidance suggests comparing those measures with the Code to identify gaps; a voluntary route does not remove the underlying legal duty.

questions.prompt: Harbour's supplier has signed the Code. Does that conclusively establish compliance?

options.blocks: An exemption from every authority investigation
options.reason: Authorities retain verification and enforcement powers.

options.blocks: A requirement to implement every encouraged measure

options.blocks: A recognised demonstration route, still subject to verification
options.reason: The assessment expressly does not make adherence conclusive evidence.
